{{short description|Mathematical graph of a Sudoku}}
[[File:4x4 Sudoku graph.svg|thumb|<math>4\times 4</math> Sudoku graph]]
In the [[mathematics of Sudoku]], the '''Sudoku graph''' is an [[undirected graph]] whose [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] represent the cells of a (blank) Sudoku puzzle and whose [[Edge (graph theory)|edges]] represent pairs of cells that belong to the same row, column, or block of the puzzle. The problem of solving a Sudoku puzzle can be represented as [[precoloring extension]] on this graph. It is an [[integral graph|integral]] [[Cayley graph]].

==Basic properties and examples==
[[File:9x9 Sudoku graph neighbors (really fixed).svg|thumb|300px|Counting neighbors of a cell on a <math>9\times 9</math> Sudoku graph (<math>n = 3</math>)]]
On a Sudoku board of size <math>n^2\times n^2</math>, the Sudoku graph has <math>n^4</math> [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]], each with exactly <math>3n^2-2n-1</math> neighbors. Therefore, it is a [[regular graph]]. The total number of edges is <math>n^4(3n^2-2n-1)/2</math>.
For instance, the graph shown in the figure above, for a <math>4\times 4</math> board, has 16 vertices and 56 edges, and is 7-regular.
For the most common form of Sudoku, on a <math>9\times 9</math> board, the Sudoku graph is a 20-regular graph with 81 vertices and 810 edges.{{r|ghmu|hm|rt}}
The second figure shows how to count the neighbors of each cell in a <math>9\times 9</math> board.

==Puzzle solutions and graph coloring==
Each row, column, or block of the Sudoku puzzle forms a [[clique (graph theory)|clique]] in the Sudoku graph, whose size equals the number of symbols used to solve the puzzle. A [[graph coloring]] of the Sudoku graph using this number of colors (the minimum possible number of colors for this graph) can be interpreted as a solution to the puzzle. The usual form of a Sudoku puzzle, in which some cells are filled in with symbols and the rest must be filled in by the person solving the puzzle, corresponds to the [[precoloring extension]] problem on this graph.{{r|ghmu|hm|rt}}

==Algebraic properties==
For any <math>n</math>, the Sudoku graph of an <math>n^2\times n^2</math> Sudoku board is an [[integral graph]], meaning that the [[spectral graph theory|spectrum]] of its [[adjacency matrix]] consists only of integers. More precisely, its spectrum consists of the [[eigenvalue]]s{{r|s}}
*<math>3n^2-2n-1</math>, with multiplicity <math>1</math>,
*<math>2n^2-2n-1</math>, with multiplicity <math>2(n-1)</math>,
*<math>n^2-n-1</math>, with multiplicity <math>2n(n-1)</math>,
*<math>n^2-2n-1</math>, with multiplicity <math>(n-1)^2</math>,
*<math>-1</math>, with multiplicity <math>n^2(n-1)^2</math>, and
*<math>-n-1</math>, with multiplicity <math>2n(n-1)^2</math>.
It can be represented as a [[Cayley graph]] of the [[abelian group]] <math>Z_n^4</math>.{{r|ks}}

==Related graphs==
The Sudoku graph contains as a subgraph the [[rook's graph]], which is defined in the same way using only the rows and columns (but not the blocks) of the Sudoku board.

The 20-regular 81-vertex Sudoku graph should be distinguished from a different 20-regular graph on 81 vertices, the [[Brouwer–Haemers graph]], which has smaller cliques (of size 3) and requires fewer colors (7 instead of 9).{{r|mwbhg}}
